intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene (139312) on chromosome 18p11.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees, the causative mutation is expected to be an extremely rare heterozygous variant, shared by all affected family members.
checks.explanation: The paper shows that heterozygous GNAL mutations cause primary torsion dystonia. The DYT25 label is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The GNAL gene is located on chromosome 18p11.
checks.evidence_quote: GNAL is located on chromosome 18p centromeric to the DYT7 locus for focal dystonia
checks.explanation: The paper places GNAL on 18p. The band 18p11 is standard location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia. It usually begins in adulthood, most often as cervical dystonia. It may stay focal or spread to nearby regions, especially the cranial and laryngeal muscles and the upper limbs, so that it becomes segmental. Penetrance is incomplete.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees
checks.explanation: The disorder is primary torsion dystonia with autosomal dominant inheritance.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 usually begins in adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: Average age of dystonia onset in the carriers was 31.3, and ranged from 7–54 years.
checks.explanation: Mean onset age is in adulthood.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 most often begins as cervical dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: Most carriers (82%) had onset in the neck, and 93% had neck involvement at final exam
checks.explanation: Onset is most often cervical.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 may remain focal.
checks.evidence_quote: however most progressed to have dystonia at other sites, and only 46% had focal dystonia at last exam.
checks.explanation: 46% of carriers still had focal dystonia at last exam.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 may spread to nearby regions, especially the cranial and laryngeal muscles and the upper limbs, becoming segmental.
checks.evidence_quote: Further, cranial involvement was present in 57% of carriers, and 44% had speech involvement. Brachial onset was not observed and eventual arm involvement was seen in only 32%
checks.explanation: Spread to cranial regions and arms is reported. The paper gives speech involvement, not laryngeal involvement as such, and describes arm involvement as uncommon (only 32%).

checks.claim: Penetrance of dystonia-25 is incomplete.
checks.evidence_quote: consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance–, but with reduced penetrance, ranging from 15% for focal PTD to 30–60% in generalized PTD
checks.explanation: The paper states reduced penetrance for primary torsion dystonia in general, not specifically for GNAL dystonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) reported several families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia. Affected members mostly had onset in adulthood, with neck involvement (cervical dystonia) as the most common first sign. In many patients the dystonia later spread to the face, jaw, larynx, or arms. Some affected individuals had focal disease, and others had segmental or more widespread dystonia.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) reported several families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: In conclusion, we have identified eight different mutations in GNAL, a novel causative primary dystonia gene. The phenotype in the 8 multiplex families
checks.explanation: The paper reports 8 multiplex families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia.

checks.claim: Affected members of the families reported by Fuchs et al. (2013) mostly had onset of dystonia in adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: Average age of dystonia onset in the carriers was 31.3, and ranged from 7–54 years.
checks.explanation: Onset was mostly in adulthood.

checks.claim: In the families reported by Fuchs et al. (2013), neck involvement (cervical dystonia) was the most common first sign.
checks.evidence_quote: Most carriers (82%) had onset in the neck
checks.explanation: Neck was the most common site of onset.

checks.claim: In many patients reported by Fuchs et al. (2013), the dystonia later spread to the face, jaw, larynx, or arms.
checks.evidence_quote: Further, cranial involvement was present in 57% of carriers, and 44% had speech involvement. Brachial onset was not observed and eventual arm involvement was seen in only 32%
checks.explanation: Spread to cranial regions, speech and arms is described.

checks.claim: Some affected individuals reported by Fuchs et al. (2013) had focal dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: only 46% had focal dystonia at last exam.
checks.explanation: Some patients had focal dystonia.

checks.claim: Some affected individuals reported by Fuchs et al. (2013) had segmental or more widespread dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: however most progressed to have dystonia at other sites, and only 46% had focal dystonia at last exam.
checks.explanation: Table 1 lists segmental and generalized distributions.

paragraphs.text: Vemula et al. (2013) described further families with GNAL-related dystonia. The phenotype was similar: mainly cervical onset, with spread to cranial regions in some patients.

checks.claim: Vemula et al. (2013) described further families with GNAL-related dystonia.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. Vemula et al. (2013) is not described in this paper.

checks.claim: In the families with GNAL-related dystonia described by Vemula et al. (2013), onset was mainly cervical.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. Vemula et al. (2013) is not described in this paper.

checks.claim: In some patients with GNAL-related dystonia described by Vemula et al. (2013), the dystonia spread to cranial regions.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. Vemula et al. (2013) is not described in this paper.

paragraphs.text: In the families reported by Fuchs et al. (2013), dystonia-25 followed an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with reduced penetrance.

checks.claim: In the families reported by Fuchs et al. (2013), dystonia-25 followed an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees
checks.explanation: The paper states autosomal dominant inheritance in these pedigrees.

checks.claim: In the families reported by Fuchs et al. (2013), dystonia-25 showed reduced penetrance.
checks.evidence_quote: consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance–, but with reduced penetrance, ranging from 15% for focal PTD to 30–60% in generalized PTD
checks.explanation: Reduced penetrance is stated for primary torsion dystonia generally, not shown for the reported GNAL families.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia and found heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene that segregated with the disorder. When they screened additional families with dystonia, they found further heterozygous GNAL mutations, including missense and truncating changes. GNAL encodes the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit G-alpha-olf. In the striatum, G-alpha-olf couples dopamine D1 receptors and adenosine A2A receptors to adenylyl cyclase. Fuchs et al. (2013) found that some of the mutations impaired the protein's coupling function.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: We performed exome sequencing in individuals from two families with PTD
checks.explanation: Exome sequencing was done in two families with primary torsion dystonia.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) found heterozygous GNAL mutations that segregated with primary torsion dystonia in the multiplex families.
checks.evidence_quote: the p.S293X variant in the GNAL gene co-segregated with dystonia in the remaining members of Fam P
checks.explanation: p.V137M also segregated with disease in Fam D1.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) screened additional families with dystonia and found further heterozygous GNAL mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: we performed Sanger sequencing of the entire coding region in 39 additional multiplex PTD families of mixed European origin who were mutation negative for DYT1 and DYT6. We detected novel mutations in the GNAL gene in six additional families
checks.explanation: Screening of 39 additional families found GNAL mutations in 6.

checks.claim: The additional GNAL mutations found by Fuchs et al. (2013) included missense and truncating changes.
checks.evidence_quote: including one nonsense (p.R21X), two frameshift (p.S95fsX110 and p.R198fsX210), one missense (p.E155K)
checks.explanation: The additional mutations include missense and truncating changes.

checks.claim: GNAL encodes the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit G-alpha-olf.
checks.evidence_quote: GNAL encodes the stimulatory alpha subunit, Gαolf
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: In the striatum, G-alpha-olf couples dopamine D1 receptors and adenosine A2A receptors to adenylyl cyclase.
checks.evidence_quote: In MSNs, Gαolf couples dopamine type 1 receptors (D1R) of the direct pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) of the indirect pathway to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5)
checks.explanation: Stated directly for striatal medium spiny neurons.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) found that some of the GNAL mutations impaired the coupling function of G-alpha-olf.
checks.evidence_quote: The p.S293X deletion mutant failed to support any D1R driven responses while p.V16F, a variant found in a single control sample showed normal wild-type like behavior. Two mutants found in dystonia patients, p.E155K and p.V137M, showed intermediate phenotypes
checks.explanation: BRET assays showed impaired function for several mutants.

paragraphs.text: Working independently, Vemula et al. (2013) identified heterozygous GNAL mutations in families with adult-onset cervical or segmental dystonia.

checks.claim: Vemula et al. (2013) independently identified heterozygous GNAL mutations in families with adult-onset cervical or segmental dystonia.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. Vemula et al. (2013) is not described in this paper.

paragraphs.text: G-alpha-olf mediates dopamine D1 receptor and adenosine A2A receptor signaling in striatal medium spiny neurons. Fuchs et al. (2013) proposed that loss of G-alpha-olf function disrupts this striatal signaling and that this causes the dystonia.

checks.claim: G-alpha-olf mediates dopamine D1 receptor and adenosine A2A receptor signaling in striatal medium spiny neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: In MSNs, Gαolf couples dopamine type 1 receptors (D1R) of the direct pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) of the indirect pathway to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5)
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) proposed that loss of G-alpha-olf function disrupts striatal signaling and that this causes dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: Identification of causative mutations in GNAL points to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission as possibly leading to dystonia.
checks.explanation: Together with the functional assay 'suggestive of a loss of function', the paper proposes disrupted striatal signaling as the cause.

references.citation: Fuchs T, Saunders-Pullman R, Masuho I, Luciano MS, Raymond D, Factor S, Lang AE, Liang TW, Trosch RM, White S, and others. Mutations in GNAL cause primary torsion dystonia. Nat Genet 45: 88-92, 2013. [PubMed: 23222958]
